item.title: Calculating Some Numbers
item.description:
Calculating Some Numbers

In order to give my aircraft feel of a true jet, I needed some numbers to add to my physics equations.

I started from the basics, Newtonian force law:

$$F = ma$$

And using vectors of all forces I get:

$$\vec{F}_{net} = \vec{T} + \vec{L} + \vec{D} + \vec{W}$$

Where:

  • $\vec{T}$ Thrust
  • $\vec{L}$ Lift
  • $\vec{D}$ Drag
  • $\vec{W}$ Weight

So acceleration using vectors is:

$$\vec{a} = \frac{\vec{F}_{net}}{m}$$

Drag - The Anti Thrust

Drag definition contain some variables $\rho$ and $A$ that will be treated as a constant to make the equation simpler.
item.content:
Calculating Some Numbers

In order to give my aircraft feel of a true jet, I needed some numbers to add to my physics equations.

I started from the basics, Newtonian force law:

$$F = ma$$

And using vectors of all forces I get:

$$\vec{F}_{net} = \vec{T} + \vec{L} + \vec{D} + \vec{W}$$

Where:

  • $\vec{T}$ Thrust
  • $\vec{L}$ Lift
  • $\vec{D}$ Drag
  • $\vec{W}$ Weight

So acceleration using vectors is:

$$\vec{a} = \frac{\vec{F}_{net}}{m}$$

Drag - The Anti Thrust

Drag definition contain some variables $\rho$ and $A$ that will be treated as a constant to make the equation simpler.

$$D = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \rho \cdot v^2 \cdot C_D \cdot A$$

In my simpler version, $C_D$ is my drag coefficient:

$$D = v^2 \cdot C_D$$

Lift - Gravity’s Enemy

Here again, list definition contain some variables $\rho$ and $S$ that will be treated as constant to make the equation simpler.

$$L = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \rho \cdot v^2 \cdot C_L \cdot S$$

And again, in my simpler version, $C_L$ is my lift coefficient:

$$L = v^2 \cdot C_L$$

Weight - Fight the Gravity

Here the formula is much simpler because I know the acceleration.

$$G\approx9.18$$

So in our case:

$$\frac{F}{m}=G$$

Numbers?!

OK, we fooled around with some equations but what about the numbers?

Let’s take somthing like F16…

Property Value Unit
Weight $120,000$ $N$
Thrust $130,000$ $N$
Max Speed $600$ $m/s$
Stall Speed $65$ $m/s$
Cruise Speed $250$ $m/s$

$C_D$

In max velocity ($600m/s$) drag should be equal to thrust.

$$\vec{T}+\vec{D}=0$$

$$130,000=600^2 \cdot C_D \rightarrow C_D \approx 0.36$$

$C_L$

In a cruise speed ($250m/s$) lift should be equal to weight.

$$\vec{L}+\vec{W}=0$$

$$120,000=250^2 \cdot C_L \rightarrow C_L=1.92$$

item.title: Getting Started
item.description:
A development or more precisely, a remake of the 1989 F-15 II flight simulator by MicroProse.

The purpose of this blog is to accompany the project’s development, document the decisions made along the way, and capture lessons learned, among other things.

I began the project by selecting a technology stack and researching modern workflows with OpenGL.

For this project, I chose a language I was once familiar with, C++, and one I’m excited to dive back into. I’m also using the “raylib” library, which provides a solid foundation and saves me from reinventing a lot from scratch.

A development or more precisely, a remake of the 1989 F-15 II flight simulator by MicroProse.

The purpose of this blog is to accompany the project’s development, document the decisions made along the way, and capture lessons learned, among other things.

I began the project by selecting a technology stack and researching modern workflows with OpenGL.

For this project, I chose a language I was once familiar with, C++, and one I’m excited to dive back into. I’m also using the “raylib” library, which provides a solid foundation and saves me from reinventing a lot from scratch.

Let’s get started.
